title: How do you safely roll out a risky feature to users?
description: Feature flags, progressive delivery, and experimentation: decoupling deploy from release, targeting rules, and cleanup discipline.

data.text: **Question:** How do you safely roll out a risky feature to users?

Use **feature flags** to decouple *deploying* code from *releasing* it: ship dark (flag off), then **progressive delivery** — enable for the team, then 1% of users by stable hash, then cohorts (internal → beta customers → region), watching error rate, latency, and business metrics per cohort against a control group. Flags give you **instant kill** without a redeploy — the actual safety mechanism. The engineering that makes this trustworthy: flags evaluated **server-side with client caching and streaming updates** (a kill switch that takes 5 minutes to propagate isn't a kill switch), **targeting by stable user hash** (so cohorts don't reshuffle), **metrics sliced by flag state** (you must be able to see 'flag-on users vs flag-off users'), and — critically — **flag cleanup discipline** (every flag gets an expiry date; stale flags are the technical debt that kills flag systems).

**The rollout ladder:**
1. Deploy dark: code merged, flag off — verifying deploy safety only
2. Internal: employees/dogfood (with a bypass header for testing)
3. Canary: 1% of real users, stable-hash assigned — watch for 24-48h
4. Cohorts: beta customers, specific region/plan, then widening percentage
5. GA: flag default-on for everyone; then **remove the flag code entirely** in a later cleanup PR

**Flag system design:**
- Evaluation rules: percentage by stable hash (user id), allowlists, plan/region attributes, and targeting percentages evaluated server-side
- Propagation: config streamed to SDKs (seconds) rather than polled (minutes); kill switch must beat user patience
- Consistency: same user → same variant across requests and devices (hash on canonical user id, not session)
- Environments: dev/staging/prod flag configs separated; flag values are **configuration**, not code
- Backend flags vs frontend flags: backend flags can kill instantly; frontend bundle flags can't un-ship JS — keep risky branches server-side

**Experimentation upgrade:**
- When rollout is an experiment, hold a control group and measure the metric delta with significance — don't 'eyeball the dashboard'
- Guardrail metrics: an experiment can win conversion while losing latency; watch both

**The discipline that keeps it sane:**
- Every flag created with an owner and expiry date; a bot opens cleanup PRs when it passes
- Flag proliferation is the failure mode: 500 stale flags = a combinatorial mess nobody can reason about — count them, budget them, delete aggressively
- Migration flags (old/new path) differ from ops flags (kill switches) — label them differently

data.title: Flag evaluation and a server-side kill switch
A kill switch you can't flip fast is decoration
data.text: If turning the flag off takes minutes (polling intervals, CDN caches, config services on the critical path), then during an incident it won't be used — people will fear a redeploy more than the bug. Stream flag updates, cache locally with safe defaults, and drill 'kill the flag' like a fire alarm.

items: Percentage rollout by random per-request draw — users flip between variants, support tickets explode
No control group or metrics split by flag — 'it looks fine' isn't evidence
Flags that only exist in the frontend — risky logic can't be killed once shipped
Never deleting flags — the codebase becomes a maze of dead branches
Flag explosion without owners/expiry — nobody dares change anything
Coupling release to deploy for everything — no dark launch, no fast rollback

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Deploy ≠ release: flags gate exposure; the kill switch is the safety mechanism
Progressive ladder: dark → internal → 1% → cohorts → GA, each step metric-gated
Stable-hash targeting, server-side evaluation, streamed updates
Flag hygiene: owners, expiry dates, aggressive cleanup
data.takeaway: The feature isn't safe because the tests passed — it's safe because you can watch real cohorts and turn it off in seconds without a deploy.
